svg.title: VolRisk platform architecture
svg.desc: Public data from Tiingo, FRED and a manual Stooq file feeds a daily pipeline on AWS that downloads, cleans, fits GARCH models, forecasts Value-at-Risk and monitors itself. Results are stored in PostgreSQL, served by a REST API to a Streamlit dashboard, and failed checks trigger email alerts. Code is tested with GitHub Actions, packaged with Docker and deployed with Terraform.
svg.text: Target design: how market data becomes daily risk forecasts, a dashboard and alerts
Numbered circles link to the plain-language notes at the bottom.
Daily open, high, low and close prices
Daily VIX index: the market's own
2. Daily pipeline: what happens every weekday evening
Runs on AWS Fargate, 6 pm ET, Monday to Friday
3. Where results are stored and shown
Only the pipeline writes here; the API and dashboard just read
4. How the code is tested and deployed
Every change goes through a pull request before it reaches AWS
Security: each part gets only the access it needs, and no passwords or keys are stored in the code.
A financial data provider whose free API (a standard way for programs
to ask for data) supplies daily prices for every asset.
The St. Louis Fed's free economic database. The VIX shows how volatile
investors expect the S&P 500 to be over the next 30 days.
A free price website. Its prices were downloaded once by hand; it
blocks automated downloads, so Tiingo is used for daily updates.
A chain of steps that runs by itself every weekday on AWS, Amazon's
cloud. Fargate runs it without a server that needs looking after.
If a source is busy, the step waits and tries again. Each download is
logged with its time, source and size, so data can always be traced.
Returns are daily percentage price changes. Realized volatility measures
how much prices actually moved, using the day's high, low, open and close.
GARCH models capture how calm and turbulent periods cluster together.
They are written from scratch and checked against a standard library.
99% Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a loss that should be exceeded on only 1 day
in 100. Backtests count how often that actually happened in the past.
A smoke alarm for the models: checks that the data is fresh, the models
fitted properly and VaR breaches stay within expected limits.
Each result is saved with the model and code version that produced it,
so any number on the dashboard can be traced back to its source.
An interface that lets other software request results in a standard
format, such as “today's VaR for SPY”. OpenAPI documents every request.
A web page of charts built with Streamlit. It reads only from the API,
exactly as another team's software would.
Amazon SNS sends an email whenever a monitoring check fails, so
problems are spotted within hours instead of weeks.
Each change is tested automatically, packaged with Docker, and deployed
by Terraform, which describes the cloud setup as code.
IAM limits each part to the access it needs. GitHub deploys through OIDC,
so no AWS keys are stored; secrets live in AWS SSM Parameter Store.
Data: Tiingo, FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) and Stooq. Repository: github.com/moumita2001-bit/garch-risk-platform
